extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write and read mathematical proofs (beginning proof-writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance for constructing and reading mathematical proofs that involve quantifiers, conjunctions, conditionals, biconditionals, and related logical structures. Focuses on strategies (e.g., introduce arbitrary elements, choose witnesses, instantiation rules), variable management, and final write-up conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving universal statements (Vx P(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a new variable x to stand for an arbitrary element and prove P(x) for that arbitrary x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start your proof with “Let x be an arbitrary element of A,” or “Suppose x ∈ A” (or equivalent). After proving P(x), conclude that since x was arbitrary you may generalize to ∀x P(x). In final write-ups you may omit explicit sentences like “Let x be arbitrary,” and you may condense or skip some summing-up sentences. When the universal is a conditional (Vx(P(x) → Q(x))) treat it as Vx and often assume P(x) to prove Q(x) for the arbitrary x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existential statements (∃x P(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose and exhibit a specific value (a witness) for x and prove P(x) holds for that value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with “Let x = (the value you decided on).” The process you used to find the witness (trial-and-error, solving equations, guessing) should not appear in the final proof—only the chosen witness and the verification that it satisfies P(x). If the name x is already used, rename (e.g., use y) and rewrite goal equivalently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using an existential given (∃x P(x)) — existential instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a given asserts existence, introduce a new name (e.g., x0) for some object with the stated property and add P(x0) to the givens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may assume P(x0) is true but may not assume anything else about x0. Use existential instantiation immediately when you have a ∃-given. Do not reuse the same bound-variable name; give a fresh variable name to stand for the particular object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a universal given (∀x P(x)) — universal instantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: From ∀x P(x) you may conclude P(a) for any particular a you choose to plug in for x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need a specific value to plug in; thus you might delay applying a universal given until a likely choice appears in the proof. Universal instantiation is most useful once some candidate a arises in the proof (e.g., an object introduced earlier or an arbitrary variable).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to apply instantiation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: General advice on applying existential vs universal instantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually apply existential instantiation (∃) immediately to introduce a named object. For universals (∀), wait until you have a specific object to substitute (a likely candidate) — e.g., in Vx(P(x) → Q(x)) you usually wait until an object a appears for which you know P(a) or ¬Q(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing logical form to guide proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the logical structure of givens and goals (quantifiers, connectives) to determine the next proof step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate statements into logical form only as far as needed to decide the next step. For example, recognizing a goal is Vx(P(x) → Q(x)) suggests letting x be arbitrary and assuming P(x). Recognize definitions (e.g., A ⊆ B means ∀x(x ∈ A → x ∈ B)) and expand them as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using conditional givens (P → Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat conditional givens as rules: to use P → Q you need P(a) for some a to conclude Q(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't apply conditional givens until you have or can produce the antecedent for a particular instance. For universal conditionals, wait for a particular value to instantiate; then apply modus ponens. Consider delaying use of general conditionals until they become useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction for negative goals
rubrics_metrics.description: When the goal is a negation and reexpressing it would require the same equivalence you're trying to prove, use proof by contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the negation's opposite and derive a contradiction (often by using givens). This technique is illustrated when proving equivalences involving negated quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable introduction and naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Always introduce variables before they are used and be explicit about what they stand for (their domain/type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State e.g. “Let x be an arbitrary element of A” or “Let x be an arbitrary real number.” Ensure variables are fresh (avoid clashes); if a bound-variable name is already used, switch to a different letter. Be careful about the kind of object (number, set, function) to avoid nonsense (e.g., writing a ∈ X when X is not a set).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding assumptions about arbitrary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a variable is introduced as arbitrary, you must not assume any properties of it beyond what was stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of the arbitrary element as chosen by someone else — you have no control over which element it is. Do not infer additional facts about it unless they follow from givens that apply to every element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating conjunctions (P ∧ Q) in goals and givens
rubrics_metrics.description: Split conjunction goals into separate subgoals and treat conjunction givens as two separate givens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove P ∧ Q prove P and Q separately. From a given P ∧ Q, you may use P and Q individually as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving biconditionals (P ↔ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat P ↔ Q as two conditional goals: prove P → Q and Q → P separately (or show equivalences via an intermediate R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may label the two directions ‘→’ and ‘←’. If the two directions use identical steps in reverse, you may present a chain of equivalences P ⇔ R ⇔ Q to shorten the write-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using definitions and expansions only as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand definitions (e.g., union, intersection, subset, power set) only to the extent required to determine the next step of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-expanding logical form can introduce unnecessary complication. Translate statements into logical symbols when it helps find the next move, but omit lengthy expansions from the final proof unless helpful for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final write-up vs scratch work
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof-development scratch work can include many intermediate analyses and searches; the final write-up should contain only the reasoning necessary to justify the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit the exploratory steps (how you found a witness or solved equations) from the final proof. You may also omit explicit statements like “Let x be arbitrary” in contexts where the strategy is clear, and you may condense multiple summing sentences into one or skip them if readers are expected to fill them in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding witnesses for existential goals
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving ∃x P(x), find a suitable value for x via solving equations, examining givens (including ∃-givens), or trial-and-error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common method is to assume P(x) and solve for x (e.g., algebraically). If a ∃-given exists in the givens, instantiate it and consider whether the introduced object can serve as a witness. Only the final witness and verification appear in the write-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiating universal conditionals effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: In statements like ∀x(P(x) → Q(x)), wait to apply until you have an x for which P(x) (or a suitable antecedent) is known or appears in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal instantiation is often delayed until a likely a appears (e.g., an arbitrary element or an element introduced by existential instantiation). Once you have such an a and P(a), you may derive Q(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using existential givens to suggest other quantified choices
rubrics_metrics.description: An existential given (∃A ∈ F∩G) often suggests a particular set (named Ao) you can plug into other quantified givens to derive conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply existential instantiation to obtain a named object, then substitute that object into other givens that start with ∀ to derive needed facts (e.g., plug Ao into ∀A∈F(x ∈ A) to get x ∈ Ao).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about the kind of object variables range over
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing variables, state the domain (e.g., integers, reals, sets) so the reader knows what kind of objects they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarity helps determine logical forms (e.g., A = B as sets means ∀x(x ∈ A ↔ x ∈ B)), choose appropriate witnesses, and avoid category errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling combined strategies and multiple summing sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: When several strategies are used in sequence (e.g., introduce arbitrary element, assume antecedent, instantiate existential), the final proof may have several summing-up sentences that can be condensed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to compress repeated summing sentences into one concise concluding sentence or to skip them when the chain of reasoning is clear to knowledgeable readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using negative givens and goals in interplay with quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Negated quantifier statements (e.g., ¬∃x P(x) or ¬∀x P(x)) often require reasoning via quantifier-negation equivalences or via contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a negated goal cannot be reexpressed easily, use contradiction. For equivalences like ∀x¬P(x) ⇔ ¬∃x P(x), use biconditional-proof techniques (prove both directions), often employing contradiction for one or both directions.
